title: UX writing for teams that do not have a writer
metaTitle: UX writing for startups, on the button
excerpt: UX writing for startups is the button, the error, and the empty state. Name the action, say what happens next, and cut the mood that hides the fact.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper. The lines are the length of a button label or an error, which is where this writing actually lives.
caption: The sentence is short because the space is. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which words matter if we do not have a writer?
faqs.answer: Start with buttons, errors, and empty states. Those are the sentences people meet while trying to finish a job. Marketing paragraphs can wait. A witty homepage will not repair a save button that says submit and an error that says oops.

faqs.question: How do we keep the brand voice without writing jokes into the interface?
faqs.answer: Use the voice on word choice and rhythm, and keep the facts intact. Name the action and the result in the customer's nouns. A joke that replaces the fact fails the moment something goes wrong. The brand can sound like itself and still say what happened.

faqs.question: Who approves interface copy on a small team?
faqs.answer: The person who owns the workflow can approve it, in the same review as the screen. Read the words out loud on the actual control. If a label only makes sense with a paragraph of explanation, the label is not done. Do not leave the words for a later content pass that never gets scheduled.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
UX writing for startups lives in the buttons, the errors, and the empty states. Those are the sentences a person reads while trying to do something. A team without a writer can still get them right. The method is short: name the action, say what happens next, and cut the mood that hides the fact.

A homepage can be rewritten later. A broken error is in the product every day. Start where the person is stuck, or about to be. If you only have an afternoon, spend it on the path you are about to ship, not on a voice document nobody will open during the build.

## Name the action

A button should say what will happen, in the customer's words. "Add company" is an action. "Submit" is a form talking to itself. "Continue" is acceptable only when the screen has already said what continues. If the person has to remember the previous step to understand the control, the label is unfinished.

Use the same verb you used in the heading of the task. If the page is about inviting a teammate, the button says "Send invite," not "OK" and not "Confirm selection." The verb is a promise. After the click, the interface should keep the promise in the same words.

Links inside a sentence can be quieter. They still need a name that makes sense out of context, because some people arrive on the link from a list of links and never see your surrounding paragraph. "Learn more" fails that test. "Pricing" or "How billing works" passes it. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) makes a related demand of page titles: they should be descriptive and specific, not boilerplate that could sit on any URL. A button is a tiny title. Vague ones force people to guess, and guessing is how the wrong action gets taken.

## Say what happens next

Every important action needs a next sentence, ready before you ship. If it works, where is the result, and what can the person do now. If it fails, what broke, is their work still there, and what should they do. Write both sentences in the design file, next to the button, so they are not invented by the first exception that fires in production.

Empty screens are the same kind of writing. Say what this place is, why it is empty, and the one action that fills it. "Nothing here" describes the database. "No invoices yet. Create one when a client accepts" describes the job. The second version teaches the product without a tour.

Helper text under a field should earn its place. Use it when the format is easy to get wrong, or when the consequence is not obvious. "We'll email this address when the report is ready" is a good line under an email field. "Enter your email" under an email field is noise. Noise trains people to skip the lines that sometimes matter.

[Google's people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a heading summarizes the page and whether someone leaves having been helped. Interface copy is the same test at a smaller size. A heading that restates the brand, and a button that restates the heading, have not helped. A heading that names the task, and a button that names the act, have. The person should not need a second search, or a message to your team, to find out what the control does.

## Cut the mood

Mood is the layer that makes an error cute, vague, or apologetic in a way that removes the fact. "Oops, something went wrong" has a mood and no instruction. "We couldn't save this invoice. Your edits are still on the page. Try again." has the fact. The second version can still sound like your company. It sounds like your company telling the truth.

Cut adjectives that praise the person for ordinary acts. "Awesome, you did it!" on a saved setting is noise, and it makes real success harder to recognize later. Cut metaphors that the team enjoys and the customer does not use. If your buyers say "clients," do not call them "heroes" in the interface because a campaign once did.

Cut length until the sentence fits the control. A button that needs a tooltip to explain its label has the wrong label. A tooltip can add a consequence, such as "This notifies the client." It should not translate the verb. Read the screen aloud. Anywhere you stumble, the writing is still a draft. Anywhere you add a joke to get through the stumble, delete the joke first and see if the stumble was the missing noun.

Brand voice still matters. It shows up as which words you choose and which you refuse, not as a costume on every error. A calm company writes calm confirmations. A direct company writes direct ones. Both can name the action and the result. The voice decision belongs in a few example sentences the team is willing to repeat. Making that list is a larger job than this screen, and it is worth doing so the next error does not invent a new personality.

## A pass you can do without a writing hire

Take the flow you are about to ship. Write the button, the empty state, the success, and one error on a single page. Read them in order as if you had never seen the product. Mark every line that could apply to any software on earth. Those lines are the ones to replace with your nouns.

Then check consistency. The word on the button, the word in the success, and the word in the navigation should match. Three synonyms for the same object are three products. Pick one and replace the others. This is editing, and a founder can do it. You do not need a style guide the size of a book. You need a short list of objects and the verb that creates each one.

Do this in the same review as the layout. Words added the night before launch will sound like they were added the night before launch. Hanabi writes them with the screen, because the label often changes the layout. A precise verb can be longer than "OK." The button has to be designed for the real verb, not for a placeholder that flatters the grid.

Give the list to whoever builds the screen and ask them not to improve the sentences in the pull request. Improvements belong in the review, where they can be read in place. A clever rewrite at the last commit is how "Save invoice" becomes "Submit" again.

## Where voice goes when you are ready

Once the controls tell the truth, you can decide the sentences the whole company is willing to sound like. That is a brand task, and it should use the same nouns you just fought for in the product. The next piece is [verbal identity: the sentences your site should sound like](/blog/verbal-identity). Write the interface first if you have to choose. The site can borrow from it.

If you want those labels designed with the screens, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio treats the words on the controls as part of the interface, not as a layer to pour on after the pictures are done.
